n: The book opens by introducing Jeremiah, son of a priest named Hilkiah, from the priestly town of Anathoth a few miles northeast of Jerusalem. He was a contemporary of Lehi, who also prophesied in Jerusalem.

f.g: A Levitical town in Benjamin, about 3 miles (5 km) from Jerusalem.

n: God’s word first came to Jeremiah in the 13th year of good King Josiah—about 627/626 BC—shortly before Josiah’s great religious reform.
His ministry continued through the reigns of Jehoiakim and Zedekiah until Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 586 BC—about forty years of warning a people who mostly didn’t listen.

f.w: the carrying away of Jerusalem captive in the fifth month

n: Jeremiah begins telling of his call in the first person.

God tells Jeremiah: before I formed you in the womb I knew you; before you were born I set you apart and appointed you a prophet to the nations. Latter-day Saints see here a witness of premortal life and foreordination.

f.w: Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee

f.g: Set apart, consecrated for holy service.

n: Jeremiah protests: “I don’t know how to speak—I’m only a youth.” Like Moses and Enoch, he feels inadequate for his calling.

f.g: Hebrew na‘ar—a youth or young man, not necessarily a small child.

n: The Lord answers: don’t say you’re too young. You’ll go wherever I send you and say whatever I command. The calling depends on God, not on Jeremiah’s age.

f.w: Say not, I am a child

n: Don’t be afraid of people’s faces—I am with you to rescue you. God’s presence would be tested often in Jeremiah’s hard life.

f.w: Be not afraid of their faces
I am with thee to deliver thee

n: The Lord touches Jeremiah’s mouth and says, “I have put My words in your mouth”—a symbolic commissioning, like the coal on Isaiah’s lips.

f.w: I have put my words in thy mouth

n: Jeremiah’s job description: four negative verbs (uproot, tear down, destroy, overthrow) and two positive ones (build, plant). Judgment comes first, but the goal is restoration. These six verbs recur throughout the book.

f.w: to root out, and to pull down

n: God shows Jeremiah a vision: “What do you see?” He sees a branch of an almond tree.

f.w: a rod of an almond tree
f.g: Hebrew shaqed. The almond is the first tree to blossom in late winter, as if “awake” early.

n: “You’ve seen well, for I am watching over My word to fulfill it.” A Hebrew wordplay: almond (shaqed) and watching (shoqed). God is wide awake and will carry out His word.

f.w: I will hasten my word to perform it
f.g: Better: “I am watching (shoqed) over My word”—a pun on almond (shaqed).

n: A second vision: a boiling pot tilted from the north, about to spill over.
Disaster will pour out from the north on everyone in the land. Invaders from Mesopotamia came into Judah from the north along the trade routes, even though Babylon lies to the east.

f.w: Out of the north an evil shall break forth

n: God will summon northern kingdoms, whose rulers will set up their thrones at Jerusalem’s gates—as conquering kings did to sit in judgment. This happened when Babylon’s officers sat in the city gate (Jeremiah 39:3).

f.w: set every one his throne at the entering of the gates

n: God will pronounce judgment on Judah for abandoning Him, burning incense to other gods, and worshipping what their own hands made.

f.w: worshipped the works of their own hands

n: So get ready—tuck up your robe for action—and speak everything I command. Don’t be terrified of them, or I’ll terrify you in front of them.

f.g: Tuck your long robe into your belt so you can move freely—“get ready for action.”

n: God makes Jeremiah a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls against kings, officials, priests, and people. The young man who felt weak will be made unbreakable.

f.w: a defenced city, and an iron pillar, and brasen walls

n: They will fight him but won’t win, because the Lord is with him. Jeremiah was beaten, imprisoned, and thrown into a pit, yet he survived Jerusalem’s fall.

f.w: they shall not prevail against thee
